newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Donors say progress slow on Ivorian cocoa reforms.
newsitem.headline: Donors say progress slow on Ivorian cocoa reforms.

text.p: Ivory Coast and international donor talks on cocoa sector reform planned for 1999/2000 (Oct-Sept) remain deadlocked but some changes agreed could be in place sooner, donor and industry sources told Reuters on Thursday
"On coffee we have probably passed the main hurdles but cocoa is a more sticky question," said one donor.
"We know there are going to be some changes next year," said a local exporter. "But we have no idea about details or timings. We are just waiting for an announcement."

Ivory Coast, the world's largest cocoa producer, has so far fought calls for complete liberalisation of cocoa marketing urged by the World Bank as a condition for a $150 million agricultural sector loan.
Exporters say some deals have already been struck but it was unsure whether they would be implemented in 1997/98.
"The messages being sent to the market are confusing," one international trader told Reuters by phone from London.

Donors see cocoa price liberalisation as the best way to ensure farmers are paid a higher percentage of export prices. They currently earn about 40 percent compared to up to 85 percent at times in countries like Indonesia.
Donor proposals include complete liberalisation of cocoa marketing and withdrawal of the Caistab (cocoa marketing board) from all market price-setting and less involvement in export contract sales.

"Farmers get less now in real terms than before devaluation of the CFA (franc) in 1994," said an industry source. "What donors want is to get the government and (reference prices) out of marketing. In effect, they are asking the Caistab to agree to be the agent of its own demise."
One Ivorian producers' organisation this week came out in favour of maintaining a role for the Caistab in cocoa marketing.
"Farmers say no to the diappearance of the Caistab," said an Ivorian Cooperative of Agricultural Farmers (CIPRAG) spokesman quoted in one Ivorian daily newspaper, Le Jour, on Thursaday.
Industry and donor sources have said they expect the government would raise coffee and cocoa farmgate prices for 1997/98 after recent high world prices.

"I'm sure they will give a hefty increase to show that under the existing system farmers get more," said one industry analyst pointing to retention of stocks into the next season for speculative purposes.
Otherwise policies remained unclear for 1997/98, they said.
Plans exporters' said they believed had been agreed included allowing local exporters to buy 100 percent of cocoa export rights at daily auctions if they outbid international traders.
Current auction rules set aside 15 percent of crops for direct sale to foreign traders by the Caistab.
Donors admit buyers at times undercut reference marketing rates but say a completely free market, with farmers encouraged to establish thmeselves as exporters, would push up prices for farmers.
Ivorian commodities markets were better structured and able to withstand a collapse in quality seen in Cameroon from 1991 after donor-sponsored liberalisation, one said.
"The government should release data to farmers on world price movements so they are aware of what is happening," said one donor. "They will not share information."
Ivory Coast set a reference minimum farmgate price for cocoa of 315 CFA, with coffee at 495 CFA.
